thesisInOneSentence: Entropy is the average surprise of a random source — and surprise has exactly one sensible measure: the logarithm of one over probability, counted in bits.
audience: Undergrads with high-school probability and a comfort with logs. No information theory background assumed. Calculus shown only as intuition. No proofs.
hook: A fair coin carries exactly one bit of information. A loaded coin carries less. The reason why is a 70-year-old formula that secretly runs every text message, zip file, and JPEG you've ever sent.

teaser.openingLine: Twenty yes-or-no questions can pin down a number between one and a million. Why exactly twenty?
teaser.stakes: That number isn't arbitrary — it's the same number that decides how small your files can shrink, how much your phone can compress your voice, and how surprised you should be by anything that happens.
teaser.openLoop: What kind of quantity is measured in 'questions' — and why does a loaded coin somehow carry less of it than a fair one?
teaser.visualConcept: Manim: a binary tree splits a range of one million numbers in half, twenty times. Each split is one yes-or-no question. The final leaf glows. Number '20' resolves into the word 'bits'. Then the title 'Entropy' lands as the payoff with subtitle 'the average surprise'.

narrativeArc.name: Teaser
narrativeArc.purpose: Cold open: twenty questions → one million → 'twenty bits'. Hook on a concrete number; open the loop on what a 'bit' actually measures. Title 'Entropy: the average surprise' lands LAST as the reward. ~6 beats, no formulas.

narrativeArc.name: Surprise is information
narrativeArc.purpose: Build the intuition that rare events are informative, common ones aren't. 'The sun rose this morning' vs. 'a meteor hit Cleveland'. Argue: information from two independent events should ADD. Probabilities MULTIPLY. The unique function turning multiplication into addition is the logarithm. Surprise(event) = log(1/p). ~10 beats.

narrativeArc.name: The bit, and the binary entropy curve
narrativeArc.purpose: Anchor the unit: a fair coin = log_2(2) = 1 bit. Then the CENTRAL animation: H(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p) plotted as p sweeps from 0 to 1. The famous arch peaks at p=0.5 = 1 bit, collapses to 0 at the certain ends. Tie back to the teaser: a loaded coin really does carry less. ~18 beats.

narrativeArc.name: Generalizing — H = -Σ p log p
narrativeArc.purpose: Step up from two outcomes to many. Entropy is the EXPECTED surprise: weight each outcome's log(1/p) by its probability, sum. That's it. Land the canonical formula and read it aloud literally: 'average surprise'. ~10 beats.

narrativeArc.name: Why it matters — compression
narrativeArc.purpose: Concrete payoff: entropy is the floor on lossless compression. Fair coin = 1 bit per flip, no shrinkage. Loaded 90/10 coin → H ≈ 0.47 bits, so a million flips can be encoded in ~470,000 bits. English text averages ~1 bit per letter — that's why zip files exist. Brief nod that the same word — entropy — also names a quantity in thermodynamics; same shape, same math. ~10 beats.

narrativeArc.name: Outro — Shannon, 1948
narrativeArc.purpose: Land the historical anchor in 10 seconds: Claude Shannon, Bell Labs, 1948, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication'. Restate the through-line one last time — 'entropy is the average surprise' — and end on the paper title card. ~5 beats.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: Concretizes 'a bit' as 'one yes-or-no answer' before any formula appears. Carries the entire teaser.
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: Viewers think 'bit' = '1 or 0 on a wire' (engineering) rather than '1 unit of resolved uncertainty' (semantic).
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — number-line from 1 to 1,000,000 halves repeatedly; counter '1, 2, 3 ... 20' ticks up; final cell glows.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: The semantic core. Once viewers feel that 'rare = informative' and 'independent events add', the log is forced — not chosen.
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: Viewers expect surprise to be linear in (1-p) or in 1/p; have no reason to expect a log.
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — two dice rolling side by side; their joint probability ticker shows multiplication (1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36); a second axis shows log values that ADD (log 6 + log 6 = log 36). The log axis is the natural ruler.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: The single most iconic image in information theory. Once seen, never forgotten. Carries the intuition 'fair = maximum uncertainty, certainty = zero entropy'.
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: Viewers might guess entropy grows with p, or is symmetric around 0 rather than 0.5. The arch shape is genuinely surprising.
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — animated plot. p slider from 0 to 1; a dot traces H(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p). Coin graphic above flips with frequency matching p. At p=0.5 the curve peaks at 1.0 bit; mark it. Then optionally overlay the Shannon Fig. 7 image from paper-md-assets as historical attribution.

conceptsToVisualize.concept: expected surprise = H = -Σ p log p
conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: The generalization beat. Shows that the binary case isn't a special trick — the formula extends naturally to any number of outcomes.
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: Viewers might miss that this is just E[log(1/p)] — a weighted average — and read it as a mysterious 'sum of products'.
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — equation reveals stepwise. Row 1: 'surprise of outcome i = log(1/p_i)'. Row 2: weight by p_i. Row 3: sum. Row 4: collapse minus sign. Contour-flash the '-Σ p_i log p_i' final form. The viewer SEES the formula as the literal sentence 'average surprise'.

conceptsToVisualize.whyItMatters: Why anyone should care. Entropy isn't an abstract quantity — it's the literal minimum bits-per-symbol you can hope to encode a stream in.
conceptsToVisualize.currentConfusion: Viewers conflate compression with 'cleverness' — the punchline is that there's a hard mathematical floor, set by entropy.
conceptsToVisualize.visualSuggestion: manim — a tape of 1,000,000 coin flips. Fair coin: tape stays at 1,000,000 bits. Loaded 90/10: tape compresses visibly to ~470,000 bits. Show the multiplier '× H(p)' driving the shrinkage.

questionsToAnswerOnScreen: Why does a fair coin carry exactly 1 bit?
Why does the log appear in the surprise formula — and not, say, 1/p directly?
Why does the binary entropy curve peak at p = 0.5?
Why does a loaded coin carry LESS information than a fair one (it feels backward)?
What is entropy actually measuring — in plain English?
thingsToCutOrSkip: Channel capacity (eq-075) — different video; would balloon scope.
The three-axiom uniqueness proof for H (Theorem 2 in the paper) — beautiful but not for undergrads-in-6-minutes.
Joint, conditional, and mutual entropy — sequel.
Markov-chain source models from §2-3 of the paper — sequel.
Thermodynamic entropy derivation — mention in ONE sentence in Act 4, no more.
The constant K in eq-017 — collapse it to K=1 silently; undergrads don't need the units discussion.
Any paperPage/highlightedQuote visual — pages/*.png have broken glyphs.

derivationsToBuild.concept: Why surprise must be a logarithm
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: If two independent events happen, the total information should ADD. But their probabilities MULTIPLY. What function turns one into the other?
stepsToShow: two independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
we WANT: surprise(A and B) = surprise(A) + surprise(B)
the only function f with f(xy) = f(x) + f(y) is f = log
so surprise(event with prob p) = log(1/p) = -log p
choosing base 2 makes one bit = surprise of a fair coin

derivationsToBuild.concept: From per-event surprise to entropy as average surprise
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: We have a number for the surprise of one outcome. What's the right summary number for a whole RANDOM SOURCE?
stepsToShow: for each outcome i: surprise_i = log(1/p_i)
we ask each outcome how surprising it would be, then weight by how OFTEN it happens (p_i)
the expected (= average) surprise is Σ p_i · log(1/p_i)
pull the minus sign out: H = -Σ p_i log p_i

derivationsToBuild.concept: Binary entropy curve in three points
derivationsToBuild.openingQuestion: What does H look like when there are only two outcomes — a coin with bias p?
stepsToShow: plug n=2 into H: H(p) = -p log p - (1-p) log(1-p)
check the boundaries: p=0 → H=0 (no surprise, you knew). p=1 → H=0 (same).
check the middle: p=0.5 → H=1 bit (maximum uncertainty)
trace the smooth arch between these three pins

metaphors.metaphor: the average surprise of a random source — the same way 'expected value' is the average payoff, entropy is the average 'huh, didn't see that coming'
metaphors.whenToDeploy: as the through-line. Plant it in the teaser title card ('Entropy: the average surprise'), repeat it at the end of Act 3 when H = -Σ p log p resolves, and land it once more in the outro.

metaphors.metaphor: one yes-or-no question's worth of resolved uncertainty — twenty bits is the answer to twenty yes-or-no questions, which is enough to pin down any number under a million
metaphors.whenToDeploy: anchor the teaser and reuse the same image in Act 2 when the unit 'bit' is formally defined as log_2(2).

metaphors.metaphor: entropy is the price tag of a random source — no matter how clever your encoding, you cannot pay less than H bits per symbol on average
metaphors.whenToDeploy: Act 4 only — the 'why it matters' punchline. Don't pre-empt it earlier or the surprise of Act 4 vanishes.

narrativeAngles: The through-line is the single sentence 'entropy is the average surprise'. Stated in the teaser title card, restated when H = -Σ p log p first appears, restated as the last words of the video. Three reps, same words.
Sequencing: intuition (surprise) → unit (bit, fair coin) → curve (binary) → formula (general) → payoff (compression). Each act EARNS the next.
Frame the binary entropy curve as the visual centerpiece. Six minutes is enough to do one animation really well; this is it.

Resist the temptation to say 'this is also Boltzmann's entropy'. ONE sentence in Act 4. The video is information-theory entropy; the thermodynamic connection is a teaser for a future video, not a detour.
criticisms: Shannon's original paper jumps from the three axioms to H = -K Σ p log p in two lines with the derivation deferred to Appendix 2. We do NOT replay this — we motivate the log purely through the additivity-of-independent-events argument, which is more intuitive for undergrads and skips the axioms entirely.

The paper uses 'log' with the base unspecified, then asserts that the choice of base only changes K. For undergrads, we must commit to log_2 from the start and say 'bit' every time — base-changes are noise at this level.

Fig. 7 in the original paper is a hand-drawn arch with no axis labels. We redraw it cleanly in Manim with labeled axes (p on x, H(p) in bits on y), tick marks at 0, 0.5, 1, and a callout of the maximum value 1.0 bit at p=0.5. The original is shown briefly as historical texture only.

The word 'entropy' is famously overloaded between thermodynamics and information theory; the paper notes this in passing and the popular literature has muddied it for 70 years. We address it head-on with ONE clean sentence in Act 4 ('same formula shape, two different stories, both correct') and refuse to chase the philosophical rabbit hole.
